intro: English has two present tenses. Choosing between “I work” and “I'm working” is one of the keys to English: this lesson brings together the rules, the signal words and the trap verbs.
objectifs: Choose between the present simple and the present continuous by meaning: habit or action now, permanent or temporary.
Notice the signal words for each tense.
Recognise state verbs that stay in the present simple (know, want, like…).
Understand verbs with two meanings (think, have, see, taste) and the difference between “What do you do?” and “What are you doing?”.

sections.titre: The main rule in one table
texte: The present simple looks at life in general: things that repeat, things that are true, things that last. The present continuous looks at the moment: what is happening now or what is temporary.
Ask yourself: “Is it a habit or a fact?” → present simple. “Is it happening now, or only for a limited time?” → present continuous.

lignes: action now: I'm walking to work now.
permanent situation: She lives in Douala.
temporary situation: She's living with a friend this month.
change in progress: The water is getting hot.
state verbs: I know, I want, I like.

texte: Some words are strong clues for the choice. They are not absolute rules, but they help a lot.
Present simple: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day / week, on Mondays, at the weekend, once a week, in general.
Present continuous: now, right now, at the moment, today, this week / month / year, these days, currently, Look!, Listen!
exemples: I usually drink tea, but today I'm drinking coffee.
He works in Liège, but this week he's working in Namur.
Listen! The neighbours are arguing again.
We go to the market every Saturday.

sections.titre: “What do you do?” or “What are you doing?”
texte: These questions look similar, but their meaning is very different. “What do you do?” (present simple) asks about your job. “What are you doing?” (present continuous) asks about your activity at this moment.
In the same way, “Where do you live?” asks about your permanent home, but “Where are you staying?” asks where you sleep during a trip.
exemples: What do you do? — I'm a pharmacist.
What are you doing? — I'm looking for my keys.
Where are you staying? — At a hotel near the station.

texte: State verbs describe a thought, a feeling, a sense or possession, not an action. We normally use them in the present simple, even for this moment.
This is a classic trap: you want to say something about now, so you think “now = -ing”. But “want” is a state verb: I want a coffee now.

lignes: like, love, hate, prefer, want, need
know, understand, believe, remember, forget, mean, think (= have an opinion)
see, hear, smell, taste (not on purpose)
I can't see anything. / I hear music.
seem, look like, cost, weigh, contain

sections.note: You sometimes hear “I'm loving it” (an advertising slogan). It is informal and expressive: don't use it in your own sentences for now.

texte: A few verbs are state verbs with one meaning and action verbs with another. With the action meaning, they can be in the present continuous.
The most common is “think”. I think it's a good idea (= my opinion, state) / I'm thinking about my holiday (= using my mind now, action).

lignes: I'm seeing the doctor at five. (meeting)
This soup tastes good. (has a flavour)
I'm looking at the map. (using my eyes)

exemples: What do you think of my new haircut?
What is in your mind now.

formule: Habit, fact, permanent, state → I work / I know · Now, temporary, change → I'm working
prononciation: In present continuous sentences, the auxiliary is short and joined: she's working /ʃiːz ˈwɜːkɪŋ/, we're /wɪə/ or /wə/.
Don't drop the -s of the present simple (she works /wɜːks/) or the short form of the continuous (she's working). These sounds show the tense when you speak.
“What do you do?” often sounds like /wɒt də jə ˈduː/, with stress on the last “do”. “What are you doing?”: stress on DO-ing.
To contrast two sentences, stress the signal words: I USUALLY drink tea, but TODAY I'm drinking coffee.
erreurs: “Know” is a state verb: present simple.
I'm going to the gym every Monday.
I go to the gym every Monday.
What are you doing? — I'm a teacher.
What do you do? — I'm a teacher.
For a job, ask “What do you do?”.
She has a new car. / She's got a new car.

dialogue.contexte: On a train from Paris to Brussels, two travellers start talking.
lignes: Excuse me, is this seat free? — Thanks. Are you going to Brussels too?
Yes. I live in Paris, but I'm working in Brussels this month.
Oh, really? What do you do?
I'm a translator. I usually work at home, but now I'm helping a team at the European Parliament.
Interesting! And what are you reading?
A novel by a Cameroonian writer. I love it. Do you know Léonora Miano?
Yes, I know her books! I think they're excellent.
Oh look, we're arriving. The train is slowing down.

mots: live in a place for a short time
like one thing more than another

items: I (go / am going) to work by bike every day.
Be quiet! The baby (sleeps / is sleeping).
She (doesn't eat / isn't eating) meat. She's vegetarian.
Where's Paul? — He (has / is having) a shower.
I (don't know / am not knowing) his address.
This week we (work / are working) on a new project.

exercices.consigne: Put the verb in brackets in the present simple or the present continuous.
items: My father ___ (cook) every Sunday, but today my mother ___ (cook).

exercices.consigne: Complete with the right form of think, have or look.
items: Quiet, please! I ___ about the answer. (think)
We ___ dinner now. Can I call you later? (have)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I'm wanting a glass of water.
I want a glass of water.
He's playing football now. / He is playing football now.
They're visiting their grandmother every summer.
They visit their grandmother every summer.
What are you doing? — I'm an engineer.
What do you do? — I'm an engineer.

exercices.consigne: Use the words to write a correct sentence. Choose the right present tense.
items: I / work / in Québec City, but this week / I / work / in Montréal
I work in Québec City, but this week I'm working in Montréal.
Do you understand? — No, I don't.
what / you / do / now? — I / make / dinner
What are you doing? — I'm making dinner.

exercices.consigne: Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) that contrasts your usual routine with what you are doing this week or today. Use at least one state verb.
items: I usually work in an office in Lille, and I take the metro every morning. But this week I'm working from home because my daughter is ill. Right now she's sleeping and I'm writing emails. I love my job, but I prefer working at the office.

a_retenir: Present simple: habits, facts, permanent situations, timetables, state verbs.
Present continuous: actions now, temporary situations, changes in progress.
Signal words: every day, usually, never → simple; now, at the moment, this week, Look! → continuous.
State verbs (know, want, like, need, understand, belong): present simple, even now.
Think, have, see, taste, look change meaning: I think so (opinion) / I'm thinking (considering).
